title: The Soundness Theorem for First-Order Logic
subject: Set Theory & Logic
statement: If a sentence is formally provable from a theory, then it is true in every model of that theory.
short: The proof system never proves something false in all models.
long: The proof system never proves something false in all models. Soundness is the converse half of Gödel's completeness theorem.
proof: Verify that the axioms are valid in every model and that the inference rules, especially modus ponens and generalisation, preserve truth; induction on proof length completes the argument.
consequence: It guarantees that syntactic derivation is a reliable guide to semantic truth.

title: Gentzen's Consistency Proof for Peano Arithmetic
subject: Set Theory & Logic
statement: Gentzen proved the consistency of Peano arithmetic using transfinite induction up to the ordinal epsilon-zero, a principle not available inside Peano arithmetic itself.
short: Peano arithmetic is consistent, but proving so needs stronger ordinal methods.
long: Peano arithmetic is consistent, but proving so needs stronger ordinal methods. The result illustrates Gödel's second incompleteness theorem: the consistency statement is not provable in PA itself.
proof: Gentzen assigned ordinals below epsilon-zero to sequent derivations and showed cut elimination reduces ordinals, so an inconsistency would yield an infinite descending ordinal sequence, which transfinite induction forbids.
consequence: It founded ordinal analysis and proof theory.

title: Gentzen's Cut Elimination Theorem
subject: Set Theory & Logic
statement: Any proof in sequent calculus can be transformed into a proof of the same sequent that does not use the cut rule.
short: Cuts can be pushed into the subproofs, yielding analytic proofs.
long: Cuts can be pushed into the subproofs, yielding analytic proofs. The subformula property of cut-free proofs gives consistency and decidability consequences.
proof: Successively reduce the complexity of cut formulas and the height of derivations by permuting cuts upward until they disappear.
consequence: It is the central theorem of structural proof theory and underlies automated theorem proving.

title: The Axiom of Regularity and the Cumulative Hierarchy
subject: Set Theory & Logic
statement: The axiom of regularity says every nonempty set has an element disjoint from it, which forbids infinite descending membership chains and supports the cumulative hierarchy picture of sets.
short: Sets are built in layers, with no circular membership loops.
long: Sets are built in layers, with no circular membership loops. The rank of a set is the least ordinal stage at which it appears in the hierarchy.
proof: If a descending chain x_0 contains x_1 contains ... existed, the set of its members would violate regularity; conversely regularity implies every set has a rank by induction.
consequence: It gives the universe a well-founded structure enabling rank-based induction.

title: The Cauchy–Kowalevski Theorem
subject: Differential Equations
statement: For a PDE with analytic coefficients and analytic initial data on a noncharacteristic hypersurface, there exists a unique analytic local solution.
short: Analyticity guarantees local existence and uniqueness for PDEs.
long: Analyticity guarantees local existence and uniqueness for PDEs. The theorem fails in the smooth category, where the Lewy example has no solution.
proof: Rewrite the system as a majorising power series recursion; analyticity lets one bound the coefficients and prove convergence by comparison with a geometric series.
consequence: It is the PDE analogue of the Picard theorem in the analytic category.

title: Pascal's Recurrence for Binomial Coefficients
subject: Combinatorics
short: Split k-subsets according to whether they contain a fixed element.
long: Split k-subsets according to whether they contain a fixed element. The two classes correspond to choosing k-1 or k elements from the remaining n-1 elements.
proof: Fix an element x; every k-subset either contains x or does not, giving the two counts.
consequence: This recurrence generates Pascal's triangle and drives many inductive proofs.

title: Symmetry of Binomial Coefficients
subject: Combinatorics
statement: For all 0 <= k <= n, C(n,k) = C(n,n-k).
short: Choosing k objects is the same as deciding which n-k objects to omit.
long: Choosing k objects is the same as deciding which n-k objects to omit. Complementation yields a bijection between k-subsets and (n-k)-subsets of an n-set.
proof: The map A -> [n] \ A is a bijection between the two families of subsets.
consequence: It halves the computation of rows in Pascal's triangle.

title: Row Sum of Pascal's Triangle
subject: Combinatorics
statement: The entries in row n of Pascal's triangle sum to 2^n.
short: Every subset of an n-set has a unique size.
long: Every subset of an n-set has a unique size. Counting all subsets by size and by direct choice gives the identity.
proof: The binomial theorem at (1+1)^n, or counting subsets, gives the sum.
consequence: It links combinatorial counting with the algebra of the binomial theorem.

title: Alternating Binomial Row Sum
subject: Combinatorics
statement: For n > 0, the alternating sum of binomial coefficients in row n is zero.
short: Equal-weight even and odd subsets cancel.
long: Equal-weight even and odd subsets cancel. The identity is the expansion of (1-1)^n.
proof: Apply the binomial theorem to (1-1)^n.
consequence: It is the simplest example of a signed counting identity.

title: Hockey-Stick Identity
subject: Combinatorics
statement: For n >= k, the sum over j from k to n of C(j,k) equals C(n+1,k+1).
short: Count (k+1)-subsets by their largest element.
long: Count (k+1)-subsets by their largest element. The diagonal strip in Pascal's triangle sums to the entry just below its end.
proof: A (k+1)-subset of [n+1] with largest element j+1 is obtained by choosing k elements from [j].
consequence: It simplifies many sums that arise in discrete probability.

title: Counting Multisets with Stars and Bars
subject: Combinatorics
statement: The number of multisets of size k chosen from n types is C(n+k-1,k).
short: Place k stars and n-1 bars to record multiplicities.
long: Place k stars and n-1 bars to record multiplicities. A multiset corresponds uniquely to a nonnegative solution of x_1+...+x_n=k.
proof: Represent a solution by k stars separated into n boxes using n-1 bars, then choose the star positions.
consequence: It counts combinations with repetition and nonnegative integer solutions.

title: Multinomial Coefficients Count Ordered Group Splits
subject: Combinatorics
statement: The number of ways to split n labelled objects into groups of sizes n_1,...,n_m is n! divided by the product of the n_i factorial.
short: Permute all objects, then ignore order inside each group.
long: Permute all objects, then ignore order inside each group. The groups are distinguished by their prescribed sizes or labels.
proof: Choose groups successively, giving the quotient of the factorial by the internal factorials.
consequence: Multinomial coefficients expand powers of sums and model categorical counts.

title: Derangement Formula by Fixed-Point Exclusion
subject: Combinatorics
statement: The number !n of permutations of n elements with no fixed point is n! times the alternating sum of 1/k! from k=0 to n.
short: Exclude every possible set of fixed points.
long: Exclude every possible set of fixed points. Inclusion-exclusion over the n possible fixed points gives the formula.
proof: Subtract permutations fixing a chosen set of k points and add back higher intersections.
consequence: It supplies the classic example of a nontrivial inclusion-exclusion count.

title: Random Permutation Fixed-Point Limit
subject: Combinatorics
statement: The probability that a random permutation of n elements is a derangement tends to 1/e as n grows.
short: The derangement sum is the truncated exponential series at -1.
long: The derangement sum is the truncated exponential series at -1. Convergence is extremely rapid, with error below 1/(n+1)!.
proof: Take the limit in the derangement formula and recognize the Taylor series of e^{-1}.
consequence: It produces the surprising e in a purely combinatorial question.

title: Ordinary Generating Functions Encode Sequences
subject: Combinatorics
statement: An ordinary generating function encodes a sequence a_n as the formal power series whose coefficient of x^n is a_n.
short: Treat a counting sequence as the coefficients of a formal series.
long: Treat a counting sequence as the coefficients of a formal series. Convergence is irrelevant when the series is used formally.
proof: By definition, coefficient extraction recovers a_n from A(x).
consequence: Algebraic operations on series become combinatorial constructions on objects.

title: Exponential Generating Functions for Labelled Objects
subject: Combinatorics
statement: For labelled structures, products of exponential generating functions correspond to splitting a label set into two disjoint parts.
short: Binomial convolution tracks which labels go to each structure.
long: Binomial convolution tracks which labels go to each structure. The division by k!(n-k)! turns the product into the binomial convolution.
proof: Choose which k labels form the first object and use the structure counts a_k and b_{n-k}.
consequence: It is the natural algebra for counting labelled combinatorial classes.

title: Cauchy Product Formula for Generating Functions
subject: Combinatorics
statement: The coefficient of x^n in the product of two ordinary generating functions is the sum over k of a_k b_{n-k}.
short: A product of series counts ordered decompositions of size n.
long: A product of series counts ordered decompositions of size n. Each decomposition is determined by the size assigned to the first factor.
proof: Multiply the two sums and collect terms with total exponent n.
consequence: It converts concatenation of combinatorial classes into multiplication.

title: Generating Function for Integer Partitions
subject: Combinatorics
statement: The generating function for the partition numbers is the infinite product over k of (1-x^k) to the power -1.
short: Each allowed part size contributes a geometric series of multiplicities.
long: Each allowed part size contributes a geometric series of multiplicities. Expanding the factor for k records how many parts of size k are used.
proof: A partition is uniquely specified by the multiplicities of each positive part size.
consequence: It opens the door to partition identities via generating-function algebra.

title: Euler's Pentagonal Number Theorem
subject: Combinatorics
statement: The Euler product equals the alternating sum over generalized pentagonal numbers m(3m-1)/2.
short: Most coefficients cancel in the expansion of the Euler product.
long: Most coefficients cancel in the expansion of the Euler product. Only exponents of the form m(3m-1)/2 survive, with coefficient plus or minus one.
proof: It is the specialization of the Jacobi triple product, or Euler's original combinatorial involution.
consequence: It gives a fast recurrence for computing partition numbers.

title: Euler's Partition Parity Identity
subject: Combinatorics
statement: The number of partitions of n into distinct parts equals the number into odd parts.
short: Splitting even parts into pairs of equal parts gives a bijection.
long: Splitting even parts into pairs of equal parts gives a bijection. The generating functions are equal because (1+x^k)=(1-x^{2k})/(1-x^k).
proof: Repeatedly split each even part into two equal halves, reversing the process by merging pairs.
consequence: It is the prototype of partition identities proved by generating functions.

title: Ferrers Diagram Conjugation for Partitions
subject: Combinatorics
statement: Transposing a Ferrers diagram bijects partitions with at most k parts and partitions whose largest part is at most k.
short: Reflect the diagram across its main diagonal.
long: Reflect the diagram across its main diagonal. Rows become columns, so row count and largest part swap roles.
proof: Conjugation is an involution on partitions, so it is a bijection.
consequence: Many partition identities follow by combining conjugation with other maps.

title: Partitions into Exactly k Parts
subject: Combinatorics
statement: The number of partitions of n into exactly k parts equals the number of partitions of n whose largest part is k.
short: Conjugate the Ferrers diagram and remove one from each resulting part.
long: Conjugate the Ferrers diagram and remove one from each resulting part. Equivalently, partitions into k parts correspond to partitions of n-k with at most k parts.
proof: Conjugating gives largest part k; subtracting one from each of the k parts gives the second form.
consequence: It lets one prove restrictions on part size or part count interchangeably.

title: Gaussian Binomial Coefficient Counts Partitions in a Box
subject: Combinatorics
statement: The Gaussian binomial coefficient is the generating function for partitions fitting inside a k by n rectangle, weighted by size.
short: Lattice paths inside a rectangle are weighted by enclosed area.
long: Lattice paths inside a rectangle are weighted by enclosed area. At q=1 it reduces to the ordinary binomial coefficient counting such paths.
proof: Encode each path by the partition under it and sum q to the area.
consequence: It is the q-analogue underlying many partition and representation identities.

title: Hook-Length Formula for Young Tableaux
subject: Combinatorics
statement: The number of standard Young tableaux of shape lambda with n cells is n! divided by the product of all hook lengths.
short: Each cell's hook length measures how many cells constrain its label.
long: Each cell's hook length measures how many cells constrain its label. The formula connects tableaux with dimensions of irreducible representations of the symmetric group.
proof: Use the hook walk or a probabilistic argument on random corner removal.
consequence: It is central in algebraic combinatorics and representation theory.

title: Robinson-Schensted Correspondence
subject: Combinatorics
statement: Permutations of n biject with pairs of standard Young tableaux of the same shape with n cells.
short: Row insertion records a permutation as two evolving tableaux.
long: Row insertion records a permutation as two evolving tableaux. The first row of P has length equal to the longest increasing subsequence.
proof: Insert entries in order to build P and record shape changes to build Q; the process is reversible.
consequence: It links permutation statistics to tableau shapes and representation theory.
